limitations: The noise and reverberation conditions used in the study might not represent the most adverse or 'unrealistic' listening situations for school children, potentially underestimating real-world effects (e.g., mean RTs often exceed 1s, average noise levels often exceed 55 dB(A) in real classrooms).
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the effects of classroom noise and reverberation on speech perception and listening comprehension in children and adults. Key findings indicate that children are more impaired than adults by background sounds in both tasks, with first-graders showing stronger effects than third-graders. Reverberation severely increased impairments due to background sounds, though it had no effect on speech perception in silence. Classroom noise had a stronger effect on speech perception, while background speech more significantly impaired listening comprehension, even when speech perception was controlled, suggesting an impact on higher-order cognitive processes. Children's self-reported disturbance ratings were low and uncorrelated with actual performance disruption, implying they did not consciously realize the detrimental effects. A limitation is that the study's acoustic conditions, while simulated, might still be less adverse than typical real-world classrooms, potentially underestimating the true impact of poor acoustics.
